criterion: Can it start with no money at all — only your time?
why: You put your launch budget at zero, so anything with a bill attached is out before it begins.

criterion: Does it start for under {budget}?
why: That is everything you said you can put in, and you named no runway behind it.

criterion: Is it earning inside {weeks}?
why: You said you need income now. An idea that pays nothing for six months is one you will be forced to abandon.

criterion: Can it sell without you appearing on camera?
why: You named video as a deal breaker, so distribution has to route around it entirely.

criterion: Can it find customers without cold calling or cold email?
why: You ruled cold outreach out, so demand has to come to you or come through someone else.

criterion: Does it work without holding stock or shipping anything?
why: You named inventory as a deal breaker, and it is also the fastest way to spend a launch budget.

criterion: Does it make money without you selling hours?
why: At the hours you have, hourly delivery mathematically cannot reach the income you named.

criterion: Does it build on the business you already run, rather than starting a second one?
why: You already have customers and a reputation — an unrelated idea means paying that entry cost twice.

criterion: Can it be run in {hours} a week, without a fixed daytime schedule?
why: You have a job with hours of its own, so anything needing you available in business hours cannot work.

criterion: Can it move forward in {hours} a week, in short sessions?
why: At the hours you have, anything needing long unbroken blocks will stall and stay stalled.

criterion: Does your qualification actually matter to the person buying?
why: It is your single largest advantage — an idea that wastes it starts you from zero against everyone else.

criterion: Does it reach people you can already get to?
why: You already have a way in with a specific group, and that access is worth more than any marketing budget you could buy.

criterion: Could you sell it to someone who has already bought from you?
why: The people who already trust you are the cheapest customers you will ever have, and the fastest proof you are right.

criterion: Does it start for under {budget}?
why: That is the money you said you can put toward this in the next 90 days.

criterion: Can you build and run it without writing code or hiring someone who can?
why: You rated your technical comfort low, so anything needing a developer puts your launch behind someone else's calendar.

criterion: Can it sell without you doing the persuading face to face?
why: You rated selling as uncomfortable, and an idea that lives or dies on your pitch is fighting you from the start.

criterion: If it fails in three months, do you walk away without real damage?
why: You put your risk tolerance at the careful end, so the size of the downside matters more to you than the size of the upside.

criterion: Is it earning inside {weeks}?
why: That is the runway you gave yourself, and an idea that outlasts it stops being a choice.

criterion: Can it grow without you doing every unit of the work?
why: You said you want to replace your salary — that needs something that keeps earning when you stop.

criterion: Does it use what you know from your field, rather than starting cold?
why: Your industry knowledge is the thing a competitor cannot copy quickly — an idea outside it throws that away.

criterion: Can you name one specific person who would pay for this?
why: Not a market or a segment — one nameable person. If you cannot, the idea is still an abstraction.

criterion: Are people already paying to solve this some other way?
why: An existing budget, however badly spent, is the difference between demand and a good argument.

criterion: Would you still want to be doing this in a year?
why: You named what you are running toward. An idea that works but that you resent is a slower kind of failure.

criterion: Can you say what it is, and who it is for, in one sentence?
why: An idea that needs three paragraphs to explain needs three paragraphs to sell, and nobody reads those.

criterion: Could you make the first real move on it this month, with what you have now?
why: Not the whole thing — the first move. An idea that needs something you do not yet have is a plan to start later.

criterion: If the first ten people say no, do you still have a way forward?
why: Most first attempts get turned down. An idea with exactly one route to a customer is one no away from over.

criterion: Could you post this every week for a year without dreading it?
why: Audiences are built by showing up long after it stops being novel, and your hours are already spoken for.

criterion: Does it earn before you have a large audience?
why: Ad revenue needs scale you do not have yet. Something you sell directly can pay long before that.

criterion: At your hours, does the rate actually reach your income goal?
why: Hours times rate is a hard ceiling. If the arithmetic does not clear your number, the plan is wrong, not your effort.

criterion: Is it work the same client needs again next month?
why: One-off projects mean starting the search from zero every time. Repeat work is what turns freelancing into a business.

criterion: Can you name the outcome, not just the process?
why: Buyers pay for a result. An offer described as sessions and calls gets priced like sessions and calls.

criterion: Is there enough of this work inside your travel radius?
why: Drive time is unpaid. A job type that only appears twice a month within range cannot fill a week.

criterion: Can you legally do this work from day one?
why: Licensing and insurance are not paperwork you catch up on later — they decide whether you can take the first job at all.

criterion: Could you cover the rent for six months at half the takings you hope for?
why: Rent is due whether anyone walks in or not, and first-year takings are almost always below the plan.

criterion: Does it work at half capacity?
why: A concept that only breaks even when it is full is a concept that fails on a quiet Tuesday.

criterion: Does the margin per unit cover what it costs to find the buyer?
why: This is the way online stores die: a product that sells fine and still loses money once ads are counted.

criterion: If someone finds it cheaper elsewhere, is there a reason to buy yours?
why: On a marketplace the buyer sees ten identical listings. Without a reason, the only lever left is price.

criterion: Can you get a first working version out with what you can build today?
why: Software that waits on hiring a developer waits on money you do not have yet.

criterion: Do you know how the first hundred users would find it?
why: Building is the part you control. Distribution is the part that ends most software before it starts.
